task_title: Minimum Safe Altitudes and Speed Limits
area: Area III. Airspace and VFR Rules
objective: By the end of this lesson you can state the 91.119 minimum safe altitudes and the 91.117 speed limits as they read today, and work out the lowest legal altitude and highest legal indicated airspeed at any point on a flight.
why: Low flying puts people on the ground at risk and leaves little room for wires or an engine failure. The speed limits change with where you are, and an ATC speed request never takes them away. Both are on the flight review checklist in AC 61-98E.

prereading.what: The two rules themselves. Read every word: the exceptions are where pilots get caught.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.117 and 91.119

prereading.what: ATC speed adjustments: units, tolerance, recommended minimums, and when you must say unable.
prereading.label: AIM 4-4-12, 4-4-8 to 4-4-11

prereading.what: Class C and Class D dimensions and the 200-knot speed rule near their primary airports.
prereading.label: AIM 3-2-4 and 3-2-5, 3-2-5 to 3-2-9

prereading.what: The 2,000 ft request over parks and refuges, and the unmarked wires and towers below 500 ft AGL.
prereading.label: AIM 7-5-6 and 7-6-4, 7-5-2 to 7-6-3

prereading.what: How to pick a safe area and altitude for low-level ground reference work.
prereading.label: AFH 7-2

prereading.what: A buzzing story told through the five hazardous attitudes and their antidotes.
prereading.label: RMH 3-3

warmup: A friend asks you to fly low over a backyard party in town so everyone can wave. What is the lowest altitude you could legally use, and what would you need to know to work it out?

key_terms.def: The lowest altitude you may fly, except when needed to take off or land. It depends on what is below you.
A city, town or settlement area. You must be 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft. The rule gives no size or population number.
An outdoor crowd, such as a fair or ball game. It gets the same 1,000 ft rule as a city.

key_terms.term: Open water or sparsely populated area
key_terms.def: Where you may fly below 500 ft AGL, but never closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure.
The airspeed on your airspeed indicator. All 91.117 limits and ATC speed adjustments are in IAS.
The main airport a Class B, C or D area is built around. The 91.117(b) 200-knot box is measured from it.
A hole through Class B airspace with set limits, used without a clearance. Speed limit 200 KIAS.
An ATC request to fly a speed, in IAS, in 5 or 10 knot steps. Hold it within 10 knots.
Distance forward for each foot of altitude lost. 10 to 1 means 10,000 ft forward for 1,000 ft down.
An intentional abrupt attitude change, abnormal attitude or abnormal acceleration not needed for normal flight.

body.p: 91.119 starts with "Except when necessary for takeoff or landing" and then lists the lowest altitudes you may fly [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. For an airplane there are three parts: anywhere, over congested areas, and over other than congested areas [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

callout.text: 91.119(a) Anywhere: fly high enough that, if the engine fails, you can make an emergency landing "without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface" [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]].

body.p: Paragraph (a) applies on top of the others. Being 1,000 ft above the obstacles over a city meets (b). But if the engine quits and the only places to land are houses and streets, you may still be too low under (a) [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)-(b)]]. The rule has no number. The test is your glide.

Glide ratio is distance forward for altitude lost. An airplane that goes 10,000 ft forward while losing 1,000 ft has a 10 to 1 glide ratio [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. Best glide speed gives the most distance. Faster or slower than that, the glide ratio gets worse [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

Your landing choices in an emergency depend on the route you picked in preflight, your height above the ground, and any excess airspeed [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. So meeting (a) starts at the planning table: route over open fields, not over the middle of town.

callout.text: Watch out: "except when necessary for takeoff or landing" is not a general low-flying pass. It covers only the low flight you need to take off or land [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

check.q: You are 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle over a large city, so you meet 91.119(b). Can you still be breaking 91.119?
check.a: Yes. Paragraph (a) applies anywhere: you must be high enough to make an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property if the engine fails [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]].

callout.text: 91.119(b): over a congested area of a city, town or settlement, or over any open air assembly of persons, fly at least 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within a 2,000 ft horizontal radius of the airplane [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].

bullets: Measure from the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft sideways of you, not from the ground straight below [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. 2,000 ft is about 0.4 statute mile.
A crowd outdoors counts, even out in the country: a fair, a race, a ball game [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].
The AFH says to keep low-level maneuvering well away from any open-air assembly of persons, congested areas, or herds of livestock [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

head: Step
Example
rows: Ground elevation
700 ft MSL
Highest obstacle within 2,000 ft
A 350 ft AGL antenna, top at 1,050 ft MSL
Add 1,000 ft
Lowest legal altitude 2,050 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]

body.p: Your chart will not show every obstacle. Sectionals typically show man-made obstacles more than 200 ft AGL, or more than 299 ft AGL in the yellow city tint [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]]. In dense areas like city centers, only the highest obstacle is shown, with the group obstacle symbol [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]]. The top is printed in MSL, and the AGL height is in parentheses [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]].

callout.text: Watch out: there is no population number. 91.119(b) does not define "congested" by size or count [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. If you would be over a town, settlement or crowd, use the 1,000 ft rule.

check.q: Over a town at 900 ft MSL. A 280 ft AGL water tower is 1,500 ft to your left. A 400 ft AGL tower is 3,000 ft away. Lowest legal altitude?
check.a: 2,180 ft MSL: 900 + 280 + 1,000. The taller tower is outside the 2,000 ft radius [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].

chunks.title: Other areas, open water and sparse areas

callout.text: 91.119(c): over other than congested areas, 500 ft above the surface. Over open water or sparsely populated areas, the rule instead says you may not be "closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure" [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]].

head: Below you
Rule
What it means
rows: Other than congested (farms, roads, scattered homes)
500 ft above the surface [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]
An altitude: 500 ft AGL or higher
Open water or sparsely populated
Not closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]
A distance bubble, not an altitude. The AIM reads 91.119 as allowing flight below 500 ft AGL here [[34:159|AIM 7-6-4a]], but every boat, car, person and building gets 500 ft
Anywhere
Emergency landing without undue hazard [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]
Still applies over water and empty land

body.p: Legal is not the same as safe. The AIM says flight below 500 ft AGL over sparse areas or water carries more risk. At and below 200 ft AGL there are many power lines and towers that are not marked, lit or charted [[34:159|AIM 7-6-4a]] [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4a]].

bullets: Guy wires can reach about 1,500 ft out from a tower. Stay at least 2,000 ft away sideways [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4b]].
Wires often span lakes, rivers, gorges and canyons, and cross the highways and railroads pilots follow [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4c]].
Many wind turbines are taller than 499 ft AGL [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4d]].

callout.text: Watch out: the open-water rule is not "500 ft AGL." Over open water or sparsely populated areas the rule is a distance from people, vessels, vehicles and structures [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]. The other way round, the rule over farmland and other non-congested areas is a true 500 ft above the surface.

body.p: Paragraph (d) lets helicopters, powered parachutes and weight-shift-control aircraft go lower in some cases. It does not apply to airplanes [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(d)]].

check.q: Over empty desert, one truck is driving on a road. How close may you pass it?

chunks.title: Rules that stack on top: aerobatics, parks, IFR

head: Rule
Altitude or limit
rows: 91.303 Aerobatic flight

Not over a congested area or open-air crowd, not in the surface area of Class B, C, D or E for an airport, not within 4 NM of a Federal airway centerline, not below 1,500 ft above the surface, not with flight visibility under 3 SM [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]
AIM 7-5-6 parks and refuges
Pilots are requested to stay 2,000 ft above the surface. The surface is the highest terrain within 2,000 ft sideways of your route, or the canyon rim [[34:157|AIM 7-5-6b]]
Ground reference maneuvers
Usually 600 to 1,000 ft AGL, with at least 500 ft above and 2,000 ft sideways from obstructions [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]
With no published minimum, 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of course, or 2,000 ft in designated mountainous areas [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(2)]]
91.13 Careless or reckless
No careless or reckless operation that endangers the life or property of another [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(a)]]

callout.text: Watch out: the 2,000 ft over parks and refuges in AIM 7-5-6 is a request, not a regulation. But some areas, such as Grand Canyon, Yosemite, Haleakala and the Boundary Waters, have federal statute limits, and they are charted on sectionals [[34:157|AIM 7-5-6b-c]].

ATC does not take 91.119 off your shoulders. VFR Transition Route and altitude assignments do not relieve you of 91.119; ask for a different clearance if needed [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5c1]]. In Class B, you still keep terrain and obstruction clearance, and you get a revised clearance when an assignment would compromise it [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e3]].

check.q: The highest terrain within 2,000 ft of your route over a National Wildlife Refuge is 1,800 ft MSL. What altitude does the AIM ask for?
check.a: 3,800 ft MSL: 2,000 ft above the highest terrain within 2,000 ft of the route [[34:157|AIM 7-5-6b]].

head: Paragraph
Where
Max indicated airspeed
Exception
rows: Below 10,000 ft MSL
Unless authorized by the Administrator [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)]]
At or below 2,500 ft above the surface, within 4 NM of the primary airport of a Class C or D area
Unless authorized or required by ATC. Does not apply inside Class B [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]
Under a Class B area, or in a VFR corridor through it
None written in [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(c)]]
Any of the above
If your minimum safe airspeed is higher, fly that minimum

body.p: Size matters. Class C is usually a 5 NM core from the surface to 4,000 ft above the airport, with a 10 NM shelf from 1,200 ft [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4a]]. Class D is generally the surface to 2,500 ft above the airport [[1:377|PHAK 15-2]]. So the (b) box (4 NM, 2,500 ft) is smaller than most Class C. The AIM repeats the 200-knot rule for both [[33:183|AIM 3-2-4c5]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5b5]].

callout.text: Watch out: 200 knots does not cover all of Class C. It covers only at or below 2,500 ft above the surface within 4 NM of the primary airport [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]. Out on the shelf, 250 knots below 10,000 ft applies [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)]].

Watch out: paragraph (b) does not apply in Class B, so near the main airport inside Class B the limit is 250 knots under (a). Only underneath the Class B, or in a VFR corridor, is it 200 [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)-(c)]].

bullets: ATC may request or approve more than 200 knots in a Class C or D surface area [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12k]].
The 250-knot limit does not apply to US-registered aircraft more than 12 NM off the coast in Class E below 10,000 ft. Under a Class B, 200 still applies [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12j]].

The military is authorized above 250 knots below 10,000 ft in active MOAs [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5b]], and MTRs are mostly below 10,000 ft for speeds above 250 knots [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]]. Expect fast traffic there.

check.q: A Class D airport sits at 1,500 ft MSL. You are 3 NM from it at 3,500 ft MSL, no Class B above. Highest legal IAS?
check.a: 200 knots. You are 2,000 ft above the surface within 4 NM of the primary airport, unless ATC authorizes more [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]].

chunks.title: ATC speed adjustments and the traffic pattern

bullets: ATC gives speed adjustments to radar-controlled aircraft for spacing [[33:282|AIM 4-4-12a]].
They are in knots IAS, in 5 or 10 knot steps (Mach at or above FL 240) [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12b]].
Hold the speed within 10 knots, or 0.02 Mach [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12c]].
Recommended minimums: piston or turboprop arrivals within 20 flying miles of the runway, not less than 150 knots; piston departures, not less than 150 knots [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12d3-4]].
An approach clearance cancels earlier speed adjustments unless ATC restates them [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12g]].

callout.text: You must refuse a speed adjustment that would make you exceed 91.117(a), (c) or (d), and tell ATC. If cleared below 10,000 ft with an assigned speed above 250 knots, comply with 91.117(a) [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12i]]. If your minimum safe airspeed is higher than the assigned speed, you may refuse and tell ATC the speed you will use [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12h]].
Watch out: "resume normal speed" ends ATC's assignment only; 91.117 still applies [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12f1]].

body.p: On each new frequency, say any assigned speed on first contact [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12l]]. In the pattern at most towered airports, aircraft typically fly no faster than 200 knots. Do the same at nontowered fields, and match the speed of the other traffic [[24:165|AFH 8-1]].

check.q: You switch to the next approach controller while flying an assigned speed. What should you say on first contact?
check.a: State the assigned speed. The AIM calls this good operating practice on each frequency change [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12l]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: lowest altitude and highest speed

body.p: **For each point on your route, ask two sets of questions.**

bullets: 1. What is below me: a town or crowd, open land, or open water and sparse land [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]?

2. Find the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft (towns) or the surface (open land). Remember the chart may leave out obstacles of 200 ft AGL or less (299 ft or less in city tint), and new ones may not be charted yet [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]] [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4a]].
3. Add 1,000 ft or 500 ft, or plan a 500 ft bubble around people, boats, cars and buildings [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)-(c)]].
4. Check (a): from there, can you glide to a place to land without hurting anyone [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]?
5. Speed: above or below 10,000 ft MSL? Under a Class B or in a VFR corridor? Inside Class B? Within 4 NM and 2,500 ft above the surface of a Class C or D primary airport [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117]]?
6. Write both numbers on your nav log for each leg.

body.p: Class B floors and ceilings are blue numbers in hundreds of feet MSL, last two zeros left off. A floor with a + is "upward from above" that altitude [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]].

head: Point on the flight
Lowest legal altitude
Highest legal IAS
rows: Climbing out over a town 3 NM from your Class D home field (elevation 800). Highest obstacle within 2,000 ft: 250 ft AGL
200 kt: within 4 NM and at or below 3,300 ft MSL (2,500 above the surface) [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]
Farmland at 1,000 ft MSL under a Class B shelf with a 4,000 ft floor
200 kt under Class B [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(c)]]
A big lake with fishing boats, no Class B above
No closer than 500 ft to any boat or person [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]
National Wildlife Refuge, highest terrain within 2,000 ft 1,400 ft MSL
91.119(c) still applies (500 ft above the surface, or 500 ft from people and things if sparsely populated) [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]; the AIM asks for 3,400 ft MSL [[34:157|AIM 7-5-6b]]
Cruise at 11,500 ft MSL in Class E
Still 91.119 for what is below you
No 91.117 limit at or above 10,000 ft MSL [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)]]

callout.text: At a flight review, the Part 91 review guide in AC 61-98E lists minimum safe altitudes (91.119 and 91.177) and speed limits (91.117) [[15:41|AC 61-98E App E]]. Bring a sectional of your area and work your own local route.

check.q: Over a town under a Class B shelf with a 3,000 ft MSL floor. Ground 900 ft, highest obstacle within 2,000 ft 200 ft AGL. Lowest legal altitude and highest legal IAS?
check.a: 2,100 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]] and 200 knots under Class B [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(c)]]. You fit below the 3,000 ft floor.

chunks.title: Risk: maneuvering low over people or property

body.p: The RMH shows how a low pass goes wrong through Steve, who buzzes friends at a park, finds the airplane won't climb as he expected, pulls hard, nearly stalls, and brushes a power line [[30:21|RMH 3-3]].

head: Hazard
Why it bites low
rows: Wires and towers
At and below 200 ft AGL many are not marked, lit or charted [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4a]]
Engine failure
Lower altitude means less time to set up and less gliding distance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]
Stall and spin
Uncoordinated flight can lead to a spin, especially hazardous at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]
People on the ground
Careless or reckless operation that endangers others is itself a violation [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(a)]]

body.p: The attitudes behind it are the five hazardous attitudes. Name the thought, then say its antidote [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. "I'll show them" is macho: taking chances is foolish. "It won't happen to me" is invulnerability: it could happen to me. "The rules are too strict" is anti-authority: follow the rules, they are usually right [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]].

callout.text: Decide before takeoff, and tell passengers: no low passes. If someone asks in flight, the answer is already made. Overfly at a legal altitude with a landing spot in reach [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)-(b)]].

check.q: Steve knows low flying is against the regulations but feels they are too restrictive in some cases. Which hazardous attitude, and what is its antidote?
check.a: Anti-authority. Antidote: follow the rules, they help prevent accidents [[30:21|RMH 3-3]] (the PHAK says they are usually right [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]).

bullets: Measuring 1,000 ft from the ground below instead of the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].
Forgetting an outdoor crowd counts like a city [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].
Treating open water as "500 ft AGL" instead of a 500 ft bubble around people, boats, cars and buildings [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]].
Meeting the number but not (a): no place to land if the engine quits [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]].
Trusting the chart to show every obstacle [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]].
Using 200 knots inside Class B, or for all of Class C [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]].
Accepting an ATC speed that breaks 91.117 instead of saying unable [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12i]].

check.q: Why can a pilot meet 91.119(b) using the sectional and still be too low?
check.a: The chart may leave out obstacles of 200 ft AGL or less (299 ft or less in city tint), and in dense areas it shows only the highest one [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]].

scenario.title: The beach party low pass
scenario.setup: You are flying a Cessna 182 with two friends on a sunny Saturday. Their family is having a party of about 40 people on a lake beach, next to a small lakeside town. Your friends ask for "a low pass so we can get it on video." The lake has a few fishing boats. A power line crosses the narrow end of the lake. No Class B is overhead.

questions.q: What is the lowest legal altitude over the beach party?
questions.a: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft of you. A crowd outdoors is an open-air assembly of persons, and the town is a congested area [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].

questions.q: Out over the middle of the lake, away from the boats, may you go down to 300 ft above the water?
questions.a: Over open water the rule lets you fly lower than 500 ft AGL only if you stay at least 500 ft from every person, vessel, vehicle and structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]], and (a) still applies [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]. But wires span lakes and many below 200 ft AGL are unmarked [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4a, c]]. The power line here is the warning: stay up.

questions.q: Your friends say, "Come on, everybody does it." You feel the pull to show them. What is happening, and what do you tell yourself?
questions.a: That is the macho attitude ("I can do it, I'll show them"). The antidote is "Taking chances is foolish" [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. The RMH story of Steve shows where it leads: a wing brushing a power line [[30:21|RMH 3-3]].

questions.q: If the engine quit during a low pass, what would the rules and the AFH say about your options?
questions.a: Lower altitude means less time and less gliding distance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. 91.119(a) requires an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]. A beach full of people is not a landing site.

questions.q: What plan keeps the flight legal and still gives your friends a video?
questions.a: Overfly the beach at least 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]], keep more than 500 ft from boats [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]], keep a landing spot in glide range [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]], and make no maneuvers that could be careless or reckless [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(a)]].

skills.do: Given a sectional and a route, find the lowest legal altitude (91.119) and the highest legal indicated airspeed (91.117) at each point the reviewer picks, and explain which paragraph sets each number.
skills.practice: Draw a local route on a current sectional through a town, under or near Class B, C or D, and over open land or water. For each leg, write the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft and the 91.119 floor [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]], then the 91.117 speed limit [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117]]. Check obstacle heights with the chart legend [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]], and bring the sheet to your flight review, where AC 61-98E lists both rules [[15:41|AC 61-98E App E]].

quiz.q: Over a congested area, the 1,000 ft in 91.119(b) is measured above:
options: The ground directly below you
The highest obstacle within 1,000 ft horizontally
The highest obstacle within 4 NM of your course
The highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally
quiz.why: It is 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 ft [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. 4 NM is the IFR rule in 91.177 [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(2)]].

quiz.q: Over open water, what does 91.119(c) require?
options: At least 500 ft above the water at all times
At least 1,000 ft above the water
No closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure
No closer than 2,000 ft to any vessel
quiz.why: Over open water or sparsely populated areas, you may not be closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]].

quiz.q: Below 10,000 ft MSL, with no other limit in play, the maximum indicated airspeed is:
options: 200 knots
230 knots
250 knots
288 knots
quiz.why: 250 knots (288 mph) indicated [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)]]. 288 is the mph figure, not knots.

quiz.q: Which airspeed do the 91.117 limits and ATC speed adjustments use?
options: True airspeed
Groundspeed
Calibrated airspeed
Indicated airspeed
quiz.why: 91.117 limits are in indicated airspeed [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117]], and ATC states speed adjustments in knots IAS [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12b]].

quiz.q: ATC gave you a speed adjustment, then clears you for the approach without restating it. What happens to the assigned speed?
options: The approach clearance cancels it; you make your own speed adjustments
It stays in effect until the final approach fix
It stays in effect until landing
It becomes your minimum speed
quiz.why: Approach clearances supersede prior speed adjustments; ATC restates a speed if it still wants it [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12g]].

quiz.q: ATC assigns 160 knots. Within what range are you expected to hold it?
options: 150 to 170 knots
155 to 165 knots
160 to 170 knots
140 to 180 knots
quiz.why: Pilots are expected to hold within plus or minus 10 knots of the specified speed [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12c]].

quiz.q: Guy wires on a tall tower can reach about how far out, and how far should you stay away sideways?
options: About 500 ft out; stay 1,000 ft away
About 1,500 ft out; stay at least 2,000 ft away
About 2,000 ft out; stay 3,000 ft away
About 1,000 ft out; stay 1,500 ft away
quiz.why: Guy wires can extend about 1,500 ft from a structure, so avoid skeletal structures by at least 2,000 ft horizontally [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4b]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, which three things govern your choice of emergency landing sites?
options: The route picked in preflight, height above the ground, and excess airspeed
Wind, weight and density altitude
Glide ratio, fuel on board and time of day
Engine type, runway length and ATC services
quiz.why: The AFH lists the route selected in preflight planning, height above the ground, and excess airspeed [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

quiz.q: A Class B sector on the sectional is labeled 100 over 40. What are its ceiling and floor?
options: Ceiling 10,000 ft MSL, floor 4,000 ft MSL
Ceiling 10,000 ft AGL, floor 4,000 ft AGL
Ceiling 1,000 ft MSL, floor 400 ft MSL
Ceiling 100 ft AGL, floor 40 ft AGL
quiz.why: Class B ceilings and floors are shown in MSL with the last two zeros left off [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]].

takeaways: 91.119(a) applies everywhere: always be able to glide to a landing without hurting anyone.
Towns and outdoor crowds: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft.
Open land: 500 ft AGL. Open water and sparse areas: 500 ft from every person, boat, car and building.
Speed: 250 KIAS below 10,000 MSL; 200 under Class B or in a VFR corridor; 200 at or below 2,500 ft above the surface within 4 NM of a C or D primary airport.
Inside Class B it is 250, not 200. On the Class C shelf (beyond 4 NM) it is 250.
Say unable to any ATC speed that would break 91.117.
Legal low is not safe low: wires, engine failure and hazardous attitudes.
cfi_notes: Have the pilot work their own home-area sectional: a town, a Class B or C nearby, a lake. Asking for both numbers at three or four points is a quick, honest check of S1.
Two speed points to probe: 91.117(b) does not apply inside Class B (250 there), and 91.117(b) covers only 4 NM and 2,500 ft above the surface, not the whole Class C [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]].
AC 61-98E's Part 91 review guide lists 91.119, 91.177 and 91.117 under Airspace [[15:41|AC 61-98E App E]]. Use it as the outline for this part of the flight review.

Read 91.119(c) aloud together: over open water or sparsely populated areas it is a distance from people and things, not "500 ft AGL" [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]. AIM 7-6-4a reads it the same way and adds why lower is riskier [[34:159|AIM 7-6-4a]].
The AIM 2,000 ft over parks and refuges is a request, but charted statute areas (for example Grand Canyon) are not [[34:157|AIM 7-5-6]]. Don't let pilots blur the two either way.
The PHAK only mentions minimum safe altitudes in passing [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]. Teach from the CFR text, not the handbook.

For turbine and airline pilots, spend time on AIM 4-4-12i: the pilot, not ATC, owns 91.117 compliance [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12i]]. For piston pilots, the point is to say unable and give a speed you can fly [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12h]].
RMH Figure 3-2 makes a good debrief: ask which attitude the pilot recognizes in themselves [[30:21|RMH 3-3]].
gaps: None of the sources defines "congested area" or "sparsely populated" with numbers. The FAA and NTSB decide case by case, and those legal interpretations are not in the uploaded sources.
91.119(a) gives no altitude. Glide ratio and best glide speed for a given airplane come from its POH, which is not in the sources.
AC 91-36 (VFR flight near noise-sensitive areas), which AIM 7-5-6 cites, is not in the sources, so its details are not taught.
Special rules for particular places (for example Part 93 or the Grand Canyon rules) are only mentioned, not taught.
IFR minimum altitudes (Parts 95 and 97, MEA, MOCA, mountainous areas) are only touched on here; they belong in Area V.

activities.title: True or false: anywhere and congested
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The 91.119 minimums do not apply to the low flight needed to take off or land.
cards.why: True. The rule starts "Except when necessary for takeoff or landing" [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

cards.s: Over a congested area, being 1,000 ft above the ground directly below you is always enough.
cards.why: False. It is 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].

cards.s: 91.119(b) defines a congested area as a town of at least 1,000 people.
cards.why: False. 91.119(b) gives no population number or size; it covers any congested area of a city, town or settlement, and any open air assembly of persons [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].

cards.s: A sectional chart shows every obstacle in a city, so you can plan 91.119(b) from it alone.
cards.why: False. Charts typically show obstacles over 200 ft AGL (299 in city tint), and in dense areas only the highest one [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]].

cards.s: 91.119(a) can require you to fly higher than the 500 or 1,000 ft numbers.
cards.why: True. You must always be able to make an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]].

cards.s: Gliding faster than best glide speed gets you farther after an engine failure.
cards.why: False. Best glide speed gives the most distance; faster or slower lessens the glide ratio [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].

activities.title: Which altitude rule?
activities.intro: Tap a place or situation, then the rule that sets your altitude.

pairs.r: Glide to an emergency landing without undue hazard
1,000 ft above highest obstacle within 2,000 ft
500 ft from any person, vessel, vehicle, structure
Not below 1,500 ft above the surface

activities.title: Lowest to highest
activities.intro: Ground elevation is 1,000 ft MSL everywhere. Use the arrows to put these from the lowest altitude to the highest, then tap Check.
steps: Open farmland with scattered farms: lowest legal altitude
Over a town, highest obstacle within 2,000 ft is 150 ft AGL: lowest legal altitude
Aerobatic practice over open farmland: lowest legal altitude
Over a town, highest obstacle within 2,000 ft is 600 ft AGL: lowest legal altitude
Over a National Wildlife Refuge on flat ground: altitude the AIM requests

activities.title: Speed limits on the airspace profile
activities.intro: Drag each speed limit to its numbered pin. Pin 1 is high in Class A. Pin 2 is inside Class B. Pin 3 is under the Class B shelf, outside Class B. Pin 4 is low, close to the Class D airport.

activities.title: What is the speed limit here?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: 8,000 ft MSL in Class E, 40 NM from any airport
2,000 ft above the surface, 3 NM from a Class D primary airport
Inside Class B, 3 NM from the primary airport, 2,000 ft above the surface
3,000 ft MSL beneath a Class B shelf whose floor is 4,000
In a VFR corridor through Class B
Class C outer shelf, 8 NM from the primary airport, 3,000 ft above the surface

activities.title: Find the number
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Over a town. Ground elevation 850 ft MSL. Highest obstacle within 2,000 ft is a 310 ft AGL water tower. A 450 ft AGL tower is 2,600 ft away. Lowest legal altitude in ft MSL?
items.why: Only obstacles within 2,000 ft count: 850 + 310 = 1,160 ft MSL top, + 1,000 = 2,160 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].

items.q: Over open farmland with scattered farms. Terrain below you 1,240 ft MSL. Lowest legal altitude in ft MSL by 91.119(c)?
items.why: Other than congested: 500 ft above the surface. 1,240 + 500 = 1,740 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]. Paragraph (a) may still call for more.

items.q: Your airplane's glide ratio is 9 to 1. You are 1,500 ft above the ground. How far forward, in feet, can you glide in still air?
items.why: Glide ratio is distance forward per altitude lost [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. 9 x 1,500 = 13,500 ft, about 2.6 statute miles. That is your 91.119(a) reach.

items.q: Over a town you plan 2,500 ft MSL. Ground elevation 1,050 ft MSL. Highest obstacle within 2,000 ft is a 520 ft AGL tower. How many feet above (+) or below (-) the 91.119(b) minimum are you?
A Class D airport is at 1,100 ft MSL on flat ground. You are 3 NM from it at 3,700 ft MSL, no Class B above, no ATC speed. Highest legal IAS in knots?
items.why: 3,700 - 1,100 = 2,600 ft above the surface, which is above 2,500, so 91.117(b) does not apply [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]. Below 10,000 MSL, 250 knots [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)]].

activities.title: Can I do this flight? The football game flyover
activities.intro: You are flying N4521K, a Cessna 172, on a Friday evening. A friend asks you to fly over his son's high school football game in town so the crowd can see you. The field sits at 600 ft MSL. No Class B is overhead.

steps.s: Your friend says, "Come over at 500 feet so we can really see you." How do you plan the altitude?
options: Plan 500 ft AGL, since it is one quick pass
Plan 700 ft AGL to stay below the Class E floor
Plan 500 ft AGL but offset to the side of the stadium
Plan 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft, with a landing spot in glide range
steps.why: A stadium crowd is an open-air assembly in a congested area: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]], and (a) needs an emergency landing option [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]].

steps.s: The stadium light poles are 120 ft tall. A 380 ft AGL radio tower stands 1,500 ft from the stadium. What is your lowest legal altitude over the game?
options: 1,600 ft MSL
1,720 ft MSL
1,980 ft MSL
2,600 ft MSL
steps.why: The tower is within 2,000 ft, so it sets the number: 600 + 380 + 1,000 = 1,980 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. 1,720 uses the light poles. Also stay 2,000 ft away from the tower sideways for its guy wires [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4b]].

steps.s: On the way you follow a river through farmland. Your passenger asks you to drop to 300 ft to look at the boats. What do you do?
options: Stay up: low flight is legal only 500 ft from every boat and person, and wires often span rivers
Descend to 300 ft but keep 300 ft from the boats
Descend: open water has no altitude minimum
Descend to 500 ft AGL, which is always legal over water
steps.why: Over open water you may be no closer than 500 ft to any person or vessel [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]. Wires often span rivers, and many below 200 ft AGL are unmarked [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4a, c]].

steps.s: Over the stadium at 2,000 ft MSL, your friend asks for "a quick aileron roll so they know it's us." What do you say?
options: Yes, it only takes a few seconds
No: aerobatics are banned over congested areas and crowds, and below 1,500 ft above the surface
Yes, since you are above the 91.119 minimum
Yes, if you climb 500 ft first
steps.why: No aerobatic flight over a congested area, over an open-air assembly, or below 1,500 ft above the surface [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]. You are only 1,400 ft above the field.

steps.s: Your friend pushes: "Everybody does it. Don't be a chicken." You feel tempted. What is the right response?
options: Do one quick low pass to keep the peace
Recognize the macho pull, say no, and fly home at a legal altitude
Do it, but only if no one is filming
Ask your friend to decide, since it is his event
steps.why: "I'll show them" is macho; the antidote is "Taking chances is foolish" [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. Careless or reckless flight that endangers others is a violation [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Over a town at 1,200 ft MSL. The highest obstacle within 2,000 ft is 180 ft AGL. A 600 ft AGL tower is 1 statute mile away. Lowest legal altitude?
options: 2,200 ft MSL
2,800 ft MSL
2,380 ft MSL
1,700 ft MSL
final_quiz.why: 1 statute mile is 5,280 ft, outside the 2,000 ft radius. 1,200 + 180 + 1,000 = 2,380 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. 2,800 wrongly uses the far tower.

final_quiz.q: You fly at 700 ft AGL over a county fair crowd in open farmland. Is that legal?
options: Yes, farmland only needs 500 ft AGL
No, a crowd needs 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft
Yes, if you stay off to one side
No, crowds need 1,500 ft above the surface
final_quiz.why: Any open air assembly of persons gets the 1,000 ft rule [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. 1,500 ft is the aerobatic limit, not this one [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303(e)]].

final_quiz.q: Over a large lake, you are 300 ft above the water and pass 600 ft to the side of the only boat. Nothing else is near. What does 91.119(c) say?
options: Legal only with an ATC clearance
Illegal, because you are below 500 ft AGL
Illegal, because you need 1,000 ft over water
Legal, but the AIM warns of unmarked wires below 200 ft and over lakes
final_quiz.why: Over open water you may not be closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure; you are more than 500 ft from the boat [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]. The AIM warns that wires span lakes and many are unmarked [[34:160|AIM 7-6-4a, c]].

final_quiz.q: Within 4 NM of a Class C primary airport, 2,000 ft above the surface, ATC asks you to keep 220 knots for spacing. Your airplane can safely fly it. May you?
options: No, 200 knots is an absolute limit there
Yes, 91.117(b) applies unless ATC authorizes or requires otherwise
Only with a written waiver from the Administrator
Only if you are inside Class B
final_quiz.why: 91.117(b) applies "unless otherwise authorized or required by ATC" [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]], and ATC may request or approve a higher speed in a Class C or D surface area [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12k]].

final_quiz.q: A US-registered airplane is in Class E below 10,000 ft MSL, 30 NM off the coast, not under any Class B. What does the AIM say about the 250-knot limit?
options: It still applies
It applies only at night
It drops to 200 knots
It does not apply there
final_quiz.why: The 250-knot restriction does not apply to US-registered aircraft beyond 12 NM from the coastline in Class E below 10,000 ft MSL; under a Class B, 200 knots still applies [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12j]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane's minimum safe airspeed in its current setup is higher than the speed ATC just assigned. What does the AIM say?
options: Fly the assigned speed; ATC's speed takes priority
You may refuse it, and tell ATC the speed you will use
Declare an emergency first
Fly the higher speed without telling ATC
final_quiz.why: Pilots may reject a speed adjustment if the minimum safe airspeed is greater, and are expected to tell ATC the speed they will use [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12h]]. 91.117(d) also allows the minimum safe speed [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(d)]].

final_quiz.q: You are at FL 120 assigned 280 knots and are cleared to 8,000 ft with no new speed. What must you do?
options: Keep 280 knots until ATC says otherwise
Keep 280 knots; ATC has authorized it
Slow to 200 knots
Slow to 250 knots or less below 10,000 ft and tell ATC
final_quiz.why: Pilots cleared below 10,000 ft with an assigned speed above 250 knots are expected to comply with 91.117(a), and to tell ATC [[33:285|AIM 4-4-12i]].

final_quiz.q: ATC says "resume normal speed" while you are flying low in the Class D surface area. Which is true?
options: You may now fly up to 250 knots in the Class D
All speed limits are lifted until you land
The 91.117 limits still apply
You must slow to your approach speed
final_quiz.why: "Resume normal speed" ends ATC's assigned speed only. It does not relieve you of 91.117 [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12f1]].

final_quiz.q: On a VFR Transition Route, ATC assigns an altitude that puts you only 700 ft above a city's tallest building within 2,000 ft. What should you do?
options: Fly it; an ATC assignment overrides 91.119
Fly it, but faster to spend less time over the city
Ask for a different clearance; the assignment does not relieve you of 91.119
Turn off the route without telling ATC
final_quiz.why: VFR Transition Route and altitude assignments do not relieve pilots of 91.119; request an alternate clearance [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5c]]. Over a city you need 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a route 1,100 ft above the highest obstacle over a dense city with no open areas in glide range. Which part of 91.119 is the problem?
options: None; 1,100 ft meets the rule
91.119(a), the emergency landing rule
91.119(c), the 500 ft rule
91.119(d), the helicopter rule
final_quiz.why: (a) requires, anywhere, an altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property if the engine fails [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]. Climb or route around the city.

final_quiz.q: You want to practice an aileron roll at 2,500 ft AGL over open farmland, 2 NM from a Victor airway centerline, visibility 10 SM, outside all surface areas. Legal under 91.303?
options: No, you are within 4 NM of a Federal airway centerline
No, you must be above 3,000 ft AGL
No, visibility must be at least 15 SM
Yes, every limit is met
final_quiz.why: No aerobatic flight within 4 NM of the center line of any Federal airway [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303(d)]]. The other limits are met: 1,500 ft above the surface and 3 SM visibility [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303(e)-(f)]].

final_quiz.q: The highest terrain within 2,000 ft of your route over a National Park is 2,250 ft MSL. What does the AIM ask, and is it a regulation?
options: 3,250 ft MSL, as a request
4,250 ft MSL, required by 91.119
4,250 ft MSL, as a request (some charted areas also have statute limits)
2,750 ft MSL, required by 91.119(c)
final_quiz.why: Pilots are requested to keep 2,000 ft above the surface, the highest terrain within 2,000 ft of the route: 2,250 + 2,000 = 4,250 ft MSL. Some areas have federal statute limits, charted on sectionals [[34:157|AIM 7-5-6b-c]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot about to buzz a friend's house thinks, "I've done this plenty of times. Nothing will happen." Which hazardous attitude is this?
options: Anti-authority
Invulnerability
Resignation
Impulsivity
final_quiz.why: "It won't happen to me" is invulnerability; the antidote is "It could happen to me" [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]] [[30:21|RMH 3-3]].
